title: Hematologic Pharmacology
summary: Anemia treatment, hematopoietic growth factors and drugs for sickle cell disease.

lessons.title: Iron and Iron Chelation

levels.kid:
Your blood is full of tiny red cells. They carry oxygen, like little delivery trucks. Each truck needs iron to hold on to the oxygen.

If your body runs low on iron, the trucks get small and pale, and you feel tired. Doctors call that **anemia**. Iron pills or an iron drip can fill the tank back up.

But too much iron is a problem too. Your body has no easy way to throw extra iron away. Kids who need lots of blood transfusions can build up too much. Then doctors use **chelators**. A chelator is like a magnet that grabs extra iron and carries it out of the body.
levels.hs:
Iron is the metal at the center of **heme**, the part of hemoglobin that binds oxygen. Most of the body's iron is recycled: old red cells are eaten by macrophages, and their iron is reused. We only absorb a small amount each day from food, in the upper small intestine (the duodenum).

**Iron deficiency anemia** is the most common anemia in the world. Causes include blood loss (heavy periods, bleeding in the gut), poor diet, fast growth and problems absorbing iron. Red cells become small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic). Low **ferritin**, the iron storage protein, is the key lab clue.

Treatment:
- **Oral iron** salts such as ferrous sulfate. Common side effects are an upset stomach, constipation and dark stools. Vitamin C helps absorption; tea, antacids and calcium reduce it.
- **IV iron** (for example ferric carboxymaltose or iron sucrose) when pills fail, aren't absorbed, or iron is needed quickly.

The body has no regulated way to excrete iron, so repeated transfusions (as in thalassemia) cause **iron overload**, which damages the heart, liver and glands. **Chelators** bind iron so it can leave in urine or stool: deferoxamine (an infusion), deferasirox and deferiprone (taken by mouth).
levels.college:
**Absorption and transport.** Dietary non-heme iron (Fe³⁺) is reduced to Fe²⁺ by duodenal cytochrome b (DcytB) and imported by divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1); heme iron is absorbed by a separate route. Iron leaves enterocytes and macrophages through **ferroportin**, the only known cellular iron exporter, and is oxidized by hephaestin or ceruloplasmin so it can load onto **transferrin**. Cells take up transferrin-iron via transferrin receptor 1. Stores are held in ferritin.

**Hepcidin**, a liver hormone, is the master regulator: it binds ferroportin and triggers its internalization and degradation, trapping iron in enterocytes and macrophages. Hepcidin rises with iron loading and inflammation (IL-6) and falls with iron deficiency, hypoxia and active erythropoiesis (erythroferrone).

**Oral iron.** Ferrous salts (sulfate, fumarate, gluconate) are cheap and effective. GI intolerance is dose-related. Each dose transiently raises hepcidin, which is why alternate-day schedules can improve fractional absorption. Absorption is reduced by proton pump inhibitors, calcium, tannins and phytates; iron also chelates and reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine and bisphosphonates. A reticulocyte rise within about a week signals response.

**Parenteral iron.** Iron-carbohydrate complexes (iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose, ferric derisomaltose, ferumoxytol) bypass the gut and hepcidin block. Serious hypersensitivity is rare with modern products; ferric carboxymaltose can cause hypophosphatemia through raised FGF23.

**Iron overload and chelation.**
- **Deferoxamine**: hexadentate, given by subcutaneous or IV infusion; risks include ototoxicity, retinal toxicity and Yersinia infection (it acts as a siderophore).
- **Deferasirox**: oral, tridentate (two molecules per iron); risks include renal and hepatic toxicity and GI bleeding.
- **Deferiprone**: oral, bidentate (three per iron); risk of agranulocytosis, so neutrophil monitoring is required.

Acute iron poisoning is treated supportively, with IV deferoxamine in severe cases.
levels.phd:
**Systems biology of iron.** Iron homeostasis is unusual because there is no regulated excretion; balance is set entirely at the level of absorption and recycling, both gated by the hepcidin–ferroportin axis. Hepcidin transcription (HAMP) is driven by BMP6–SMAD signaling, which is tuned by the iron-sensing complex of HFE, transferrin receptor 2 and hemojuvelin, and is cleaved down by matriptase-2 (TMPRSS6). Inflammation induces hepcidin through IL-6–JAK–STAT3, producing the iron-restricted erythropoiesis of anemia of inflammation. Erythroferrone from erythroblasts sequesters BMPs to suppress hepcidin, which explains why ineffective erythropoiesis in non-transfused β-thalassemia causes iron loading even without transfusions.

Cellular iron is coordinated post-transcriptionally by iron-regulatory proteins (IRP1/2) binding iron-responsive elements: in iron deficiency they stabilize transferrin receptor mRNA and block ferritin translation.

**Pharmacologic consequences.** Because oral iron raises hepcidin for roughly a day, studies in iron-deficient women showed that alternate-day administration improves fractional absorption, challenging traditional multiple-daily regimens. In inflammatory states (chronic kidney disease, IBD, cancer), high hepcidin blunts oral iron, favoring IV routes. Hepcidin-targeting strategies (hepcidin mimetics such as rusfertide for polycythemia vera and thalassemia; anti-hepcidin and BMP-pathway inhibitors for anemia of inflammation) are an active research area.

**Chelator chemistry.** Fe³⁺ prefers six hard oxygen donors in an octahedral geometry. Denticity determines stoichiometry: deferoxamine (hexadentate hydroxamate, 1:1), deferasirox (tridentate, 2:1) and deferiprone (bidentate 3-hydroxypyridin-4-one, 3:1). Lower-denticity chelators can form incomplete complexes at low concentration that may be redox-active. Small, neutral deferiprone penetrates cells well and is particularly effective at removing cardiac iron, while deferoxamine's short half-life demands prolonged infusion. Combination regimens exploit a shuttle effect: an intracellular chelator hands iron to a plasma chelator for excretion. Cardiac T2* MRI quantifies myocardial iron and has reshaped chelation targeting.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosing the deficit correctly.** Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so a normal value does not rule out iron deficiency in inflammation; transferrin saturation, soluble transferrin receptor and reticulocyte hemoglobin content help. A clinician never stops at "iron deficiency": in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman, unexplained iron deficiency means looking for gastrointestinal blood loss, including cancer, and testing for celiac disease. In adolescents, rapid growth, menstruation and diet are common causes, but the same rule applies if the story doesn't fit.

**Choosing a route.** Oral iron first for most stable patients. Switch to IV iron for intolerance, malabsorption (celiac disease, bariatric surgery), ongoing losses exceeding absorption, chronic kidney disease on erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, inflammatory bowel disease, late pregnancy, or when a rapid repletion is needed before surgery (patient blood management). Watch for infusion reactions, often minor (Fishbane reactions) and not true anaphylaxis, and check phosphate after repeated ferric carboxymaltose.

**Interactions to remember.** Separate iron from levothyroxine, tetracyclines, quinolones, bisphosphonates and some HIV integrase inhibitors. Black stools from iron are expected but are typically not tarry or sticky like melena.

**Iron poisoning in children.** Iron tablets are a classic cause of serious pediatric poisoning because they look like sweets. Stages run from GI injury and bleeding, through a deceptive quiet phase, to shock, metabolic acidosis and liver failure, with late gastric outlet scarring. Radiopaque tablets may appear on an X-ray. Management is supportive care plus IV deferoxamine for systemic toxicity; poison center guidance is standard. Child-resistant packaging cut deaths dramatically.

**Chelation practice.** In transfusion-dependent thalassemia or sickle cell disease, monitor ferritin trends, liver iron concentration by MRI and cardiac T2*. Tailor the chelator to the organ at risk (deferiprone or combination therapy for cardiac siderosis), and monitor creatinine and liver enzymes on deferasirox and neutrophil counts on deferiprone.

keyPoints: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin to block iron absorption and recycling
Iron deficiency: microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low ferritin
Oral ferrous salts first; IV iron for intolerance, malabsorption or inflammation
No regulated iron excretion, so transfusions cause overload
Chelators: deferoxamine (infusion), deferasirox and deferiprone (oral)
Deferoxamine is the antidote for severe iron poisoning

test.q: Which protein is the only known cellular iron exporter?
test.explain: Ferroportin exports iron from enterocytes and macrophages; transferrin carries iron in plasma and ferritin stores it.

test.q: Hepcidin lowers plasma iron by:
test.explain: Hepcidin binds ferroportin and triggers its destruction, trapping iron inside cells.

test.q: Which lab is the most specific single marker of low iron stores (without inflammation)?
test.explain: Ferritin reflects stores; a low value is very specific for iron deficiency. High MCV suggests B12/folate deficiency instead.

test.q: Iron deficiency anemia typically produces red cells that are:
test.explain: Lack of iron limits hemoglobin synthesis, so cells are small and pale.

test.q: Which taken with oral iron increases its absorption?
test.explain: Ascorbic acid keeps iron in the reduced Fe²⁺ form; the others reduce absorption.

test.q: Which chelator carries a risk of agranulocytosis, requiring neutrophil monitoring?
test.explain: Deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis; deferasirox mainly affects kidney and liver; deferoxamine affects hearing and vision.

test.q: Which chelator is given as an infusion and can predispose to Yersinia infection?
test.explain: Deferoxamine acts like a siderophore that Yersinia can use to obtain iron.

test.q: Why does inflammation cause poor response to oral iron?
choices: IL-6 raises hepcidin, blocking iron export from enterocytes
test.explain: IL-6 induces hepcidin, which shuts ferroportin and blocks absorption.

test.q: Name the liver hormone that is the master regulator of iron balance.
test.explain: Hepcidin controls absorption and recycling by degrading ferroportin.

test.q: Iron is stored inside cells bound to the protein ___.
test.explain: Ferritin stores iron; serum ferritin estimates body stores.

test.q: Iron travels in the blood bound to ___.
test.explain: Transferrin carries Fe³⁺ in plasma to cells with transferrin receptors.

test.q: What is the antidote for severe acute iron poisoning?
test.explain: IV deferoxamine chelates free iron in systemic iron toxicity, along with supportive care.

kidTest.q: What do red blood cells carry?
kidTest.explain: Red cells carry oxygen around your body.

kidTest.q: What metal helps red cells hold oxygen?
kidTest.explain: Iron sits in the middle of hemoglobin and grabs oxygen.

kidTest.q: Not enough healthy red cells is called:
kidTest.explain: Anemia means too few or weak red cells, so you feel tired.

kidTest.q: What does a chelator do?
choices: Grabs extra iron so it can leave the body
kidTest.explain: A chelator is like a magnet that pulls extra iron out.

kidTest.q: When you are low on iron you often feel ___.
kidTest.explain: Without enough iron, less oxygen gets delivered, so you feel tired.

advancedTest.q: Why does non-transfused β-thalassemia still cause iron overload?
choices: Erythroferrone from expanded erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin, increasing absorption
advancedTest.explain: Ineffective erythropoiesis produces erythroferrone, which lowers hepcidin so the gut absorbs excess iron.

advancedTest.q: Why can alternate-day oral iron improve fractional absorption?
choices: It avoids the hepcidin rise that follows each dose
advancedTest.explain: Each dose raises hepcidin for about a day; spacing doses lets hepcidin fall back.

advancedTest.q: Deferasirox binds Fe³⁺ in a 2:1 ratio because it is:
advancedTest.explain: Fe³⁺ needs six donor atoms; two tridentate molecules fill the octahedral sphere.

advancedTest.q: An adult man has new iron deficiency anemia with no obvious cause. The key next step is:
choices: Iron pills and no further workup
advancedTest.explain: Unexplained iron deficiency in a man needs GI evaluation for bleeding, including cancer.

lessons.title: Vitamin B12 and Folate

levels.kid:
Your body makes new red blood cells every day, like a bakery baking bread. To bake, it needs two special helpers: **vitamin B12** and **folate**.

These helpers let cells copy their instructions (DNA) so they can split into new cells. Without them, the red cells come out too big and clumsy, and there aren't enough of them. You feel tired.

B12 comes from foods like meat, eggs and milk. Folate comes from leafy greens and beans. B12 is also important for your nerves. If someone can't absorb B12 from food, doctors can give it as a shot.
levels.hs:
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate (vitamin B9) are both needed to make DNA. Rapidly dividing cells, like those in the bone marrow, are hit first when either is missing. The result is **megaloblastic anemia**: big red cells (macrocytic, high MCV) and neutrophils with too many lobes (hypersegmented).

**B12** comes only from animal foods (or fortified foods). To absorb it, the stomach makes **intrinsic factor**, which carries B12 to the end of the small intestine (the ileum). Causes of deficiency:
- **Pernicious anemia**: an autoimmune attack on the cells that make intrinsic factor.
- Vegan diets without supplements, stomach or ileum surgery, Crohn disease, and long-term metformin or acid-suppressing drugs.

B12 deficiency can also damage the spinal cord and nerves (numbness, poor balance, memory problems), sometimes before anemia appears.

**Folate** comes from leafy greens, legumes and fortified grains. Deficiency is caused by poor diet, pregnancy, some drugs (methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin) and malabsorption. Folic acid before and during early pregnancy prevents **neural tube defects** such as spina bifida.

**Treatment**: B12 by injection (hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin) or high-dose oral tablets; folic acid tablets. Giving folate alone to someone low in B12 can fix the anemia but let nerve damage continue, so B12 is always checked.
levels.college:
**Biochemistry.** 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) donates its methyl group to homocysteine to form methionine, catalyzed by **methionine synthase**, which requires methylcobalamin. Without B12, folate becomes trapped as 5-MTHF (the **methyl-folate trap**), starving thymidylate synthesis of 5,10-methylene-THF; uracil is misincorporated into DNA, and nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasmic maturation, producing megaloblasts. The second B12 enzyme, **methylmalonyl-CoA mutase** (adenosylcobalamin), converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.

**Labs.** Both deficiencies raise homocysteine; only B12 deficiency raises **methylmalonic acid (MMA)**. Serum B12 levels can be misleading; MMA and homocysteine help in borderline cases. Pernicious anemia shows anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies.

**Absorption of B12.** Released from food by acid and pepsin, bound by haptocorrin, freed by pancreatic proteases, then bound to intrinsic factor and taken up by the cubilin receptor in the terminal ileum. About one percent is absorbed by passive diffusion independent of intrinsic factor, which is why high-dose oral B12 can work even in pernicious anemia.

**Drug-induced deficiency.**
- Folate antagonists: methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor), trimethoprim and pyrimethamine (weak human DHFR inhibition), phenytoin and other anticonvulsants.
- B12: metformin (impaired ileal uptake), proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers (reduced food-cobalamin release).

**Therapy.** Hydroxocobalamin is retained longer than cyanocobalamin. During repletion, the marrow surge can drop potassium (hypokalemia) and unmask iron deficiency. Reticulocytes rise within days. Leucovorin (folinic acid) is already reduced, bypassing DHFR, so it rescues normal cells after high-dose methotrexate; folic acid cannot do this. Neurological damage from B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts) may be only partly reversible, making early treatment critical.
levels.phd:
**Why the neurology?** Subacute combined degeneration affects the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts with intramyelinic vacuolation. The mechanism remains debated: reduced methionine synthase activity lowers S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor needed for myelin protein and phospholipid methylation; accumulation of methylmalonyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA may produce abnormal odd-chain and branched fatty acids incorporated into myelin; and altered cytokine and growth factor balance (for example TNF-α and epidermal growth factor) has been proposed. Folate deficiency rarely produces the same lesion, implicating the mutase pathway or SAM depletion specific to cobalamin.

**The folate cycle as a drug target.** Folate metabolism is among the most successfully drugged pathways: DHFR (methotrexate, pemetrexed partially, trimethoprim in bacteria, pyrimethamine in protozoa), thymidylate synthase (5-fluorouracil via FdUMP, pemetrexed) and GAR/AICAR transformylases (pemetrexed). Selectivity in antimicrobials comes from differences in DHFR binding: trimethoprim binds bacterial DHFR many thousand-fold more tightly than human DHFR. Bacteria synthesize folate de novo, which sulfonamides block; humans rely on dietary folate, transported by the reduced folate carrier and proton-coupled folate transporter (PCFT, mutated in hereditary folate malabsorption).

**Polyglutamation.** Folates and methotrexate are retained intracellularly by folylpolyglutamate synthetase, which adds glutamate residues; this increases target affinity and duration, and loss of polyglutamation is a mechanism of methotrexate resistance.

**MTHFR polymorphism.** The C677T variant produces a thermolabile enzyme with modestly raised homocysteine when folate is low; despite popular claims, routine testing is not recommended because it does not predict clinically meaningful outcomes.

**Public health pharmacology.** Mandatory folic acid fortification of grain reduced neural tube defects substantially in many countries, illustrating population-level pharmacology. Debate continues about unmetabolized folic acid and about masking B12 deficiency in older adults.
levels.expert:
**Clinical recognition.** Think B12 deficiency in anyone with macrocytosis, unexplained neuropathy, gait ataxia, cognitive change or glossitis, and remember that the neurology can occur with a normal hemoglobin and even normal MCV, especially when coexisting iron deficiency or thalassemia trait masks macrocytosis. A positive Romberg sign and loss of vibration and joint position sense point to dorsal column disease. Severe megaloblastic anemia can mimic hemolysis or even leukemia: high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin and pancytopenia from intramedullary destruction.

**Treatment logic.**
- With neurological involvement, start parenteral B12 promptly and intensively; do not wait for confirmatory antibody tests.
- Never treat suspected combined deficiency with folic acid alone.
- Pernicious anemia needs lifelong replacement, and the patient has a higher risk of gastric cancer and neuroendocrine tumors.
- High-dose oral B12 is an evidence-based alternative to injections in many patients without severe neurology.
- After bariatric surgery, lifelong supplementation and monitoring are routine.

**Drug-related deficiency.** Check B12 periodically in long-term metformin users, particularly those with neuropathy, which may otherwise be blamed on diabetes. Patients on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis usually take folic acid supplementation to reduce mucositis and liver toxicity without losing efficacy. Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and valproate increase folate needs, which matters in pregnancy planning.

**Methotrexate rescue.** After high-dose methotrexate for cancer, leucovorin rescue is timed by drug level monitoring. In toxicity with renal failure, glucarpidase, a bacterial enzyme that cleaves methotrexate, rapidly lowers plasma levels.

**Pitfalls.** Monitor potassium in the first days of treating severe megaloblastic anemia, and anticipate unmasked iron deficiency as the marrow ramps up. Serum B12 assays can give falsely normal results in pernicious anemia because of anti-intrinsic factor antibody interference; if the clinical picture fits, check MMA and treat.

keyPoints: B12 and folate are needed for DNA synthesis; deficiency gives megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia
B12 needs intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum; pernicious anemia is autoimmune
MMA rises only in B12 deficiency; homocysteine rises in both
B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration
Never give folate alone in possible B12 deficiency
Leucovorin bypasses DHFR to rescue cells after methotrexate

test.q: Megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency causes red cells that are:
test.explain: Impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation, producing large cells with a high MCV.

test.q: Intrinsic factor is made by which cells?
test.explain: Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor; autoimmune loss causes pernicious anemia.

test.q: B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed in the:
test.explain: Cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum take up the IF–B12 complex; iron is absorbed in the duodenum.

test.q: Which lab is raised in B12 deficiency but NOT in pure folate deficiency?
test.explain: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires B12 only, so MMA rises only in B12 deficiency.

test.q: Which finding is typical of megaloblastic anemia on a blood smear?
test.explain: Neutrophils with six or more lobes are a classic sign.

test.q: Which drug inhibits dihydrofolate reductase?
test.explain: Methotrexate blocks DHFR; metformin and omeprazole reduce B12 absorption instead.

test.q: Why is folic acid alone dangerous in undiagnosed B12 deficiency?
choices: It corrects the anemia but lets nerve damage progress
test.explain: Folate can bypass the methyl-folate trap for DNA synthesis but does not fix the B12-dependent neurological damage.

test.q: Folic acid supplementation before pregnancy reduces the risk of:
test.explain: Folate is critical for neural tube closure in early pregnancy.

test.q: Which form rescues normal cells after high-dose methotrexate?
test.explain: Leucovorin is already reduced, so it bypasses the blocked DHFR enzyme.

test.q: The autoimmune disease that destroys intrinsic factor production is ___ anemia.
test.explain: Pernicious anemia is the classic cause of B12 malabsorption.

test.q: Which enzyme needs both methylcobalamin and 5-methyl-THF?
test.explain: Methionine synthase converts homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-MTHF via B12.

test.q: B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts in subacute combined ___.
test.explain: Subacute combined degeneration causes loss of vibration/position sense and weakness.

kidTest.q: What do B12 and folate help your body make?
kidTest.explain: They help make DNA so new blood cells can form.

kidTest.q: Without enough B12 or folate, red cells come out:
kidTest.explain: They grow too big and there aren't enough of them.

kidTest.q: Which food has lots of folate?
kidTest.explain: Spinach and other leafy greens are full of folate.

kidTest.q: B12 also helps keep your ___ healthy.
kidTest.explain: B12 protects your nerves and spinal cord.

kidTest.q: If someone can't absorb B12, doctors can give it as a ___.
kidTest.explain: An injection skips the gut.

advancedTest.q: The 'methyl-folate trap' explains megaloblastic anemia in B12 deficiency because:
choices: Folate gets stuck as 5-MTHF and cannot regenerate THF for thymidylate synthesis
advancedTest.explain: Without methionine synthase, 5-MTHF can't be demethylated, starving DNA synthesis of folate cofactors.

advancedTest.q: A patient starting treatment for severe megaloblastic anemia should be monitored early for:
advancedTest.explain: The burst of new cell production pulls potassium into cells.

advancedTest.q: How can high-dose oral B12 work in pernicious anemia?
choices: It is absorbed in the stomach as a complex with acid
About 1% is absorbed by passive diffusion independent of intrinsic factor
advancedTest.explain: Passive, IF-independent diffusion allows adequate absorption when oral intake is high.

advancedTest.q: Which enzyme is used to rapidly lower toxic methotrexate levels in renal failure?
advancedTest.explain: Glucarpidase cleaves methotrexate into inactive metabolites.

lessons.title: Hematopoietic Growth Factors

levels.kid:
Deep inside your bones is soft stuff called **marrow**. It is a factory that makes your blood cells.

The factory listens for messages. When your kidneys notice there isn't enough oxygen, they send a message called **EPO** that says, "Make more red cells!" Other messages say, "Make more germ-fighting white cells!" or "Make more platelets to stop bleeding!"

Doctors can make these messages in a lab. They give them to people whose factory is slow, like people with sick kidneys or people getting strong cancer medicine. It's like turning up the volume on the factory's radio.
levels.hs:
Blood cells all come from **hematopoietic stem cells** in the bone marrow. Hormone-like proteins called **growth factors** tell these cells which type to become and how many to make.

- **Erythropoietin (EPO)** is made mainly by the kidneys when they sense low oxygen. It drives red cell production. Lab-made versions are called **erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs)**: epoetin alfa and darbepoetin. They treat anemia from chronic kidney disease and some anemia caused by chemotherapy.
- **G-CSF** (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) boosts neutrophils, the white cells that fight bacteria. Filgrastim and pegfilgrastim prevent dangerous infections after chemotherapy and help collect stem cells for transplants. Bone pain is the common side effect.
- **Thrombopoietin (TPO)** controls platelet production. **TPO receptor agonists** (romiplostim, eltrombopag) raise platelets in immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

There are newer drugs too. **HIF-PH inhibitors** such as daprodustat are pills that trick the body into thinking oxygen is low, so it makes its own EPO.

Risks matter. ESAs that push hemoglobin too high increase the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart problems, so doctors aim for a partial correction. ESAs only work if there is enough iron, so iron is checked first.
levels.college:
**Receptors and signaling.** The EPO receptor and TPO receptor (c-Mpl) are type I cytokine receptors without intrinsic kinase activity; ligand binding repositions preformed receptor dimers and activates **JAK2**, which phosphorylates STAT5 and engages PI3K–AKT and MAPK pathways. EPO mainly prevents apoptosis of CFU-E and proerythroblasts. The acquired JAK2 V617F mutation constitutively activates this pathway in polycythemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms. G-CSF signals through its own receptor (CSF3R) via JAK–STAT, increasing neutrophil production, accelerating maturation and mobilizing neutrophils and stem cells (partly by cleaving CXCR4–CXCL12 retention signals).

**ESAs.**
- Epoetin alfa: recombinant EPO, short half-life.
- Darbepoetin alfa: extra N-linked glycosylation sites, more sialic acid, longer half-life, so less frequent dosing.
- Methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoetin beta: continuous receptor activator with a very long half-life.
Adverse effects: hypertension, thrombosis (including dialysis access), stroke and possible tumor progression in some cancers. Trials (CHOIR, CREATE, TREAT) showed harm when targeting near-normal hemoglobin in CKD. Hyporesponse usually means iron deficiency, inflammation, infection, hyperparathyroidism or inadequate dialysis. Rarely, anti-EPO antibodies cause **pure red cell aplasia**.

**HIF-PH inhibitors** (roxadustat, daprodustat, vadadustat) inhibit prolyl hydroxylase domain enzymes that normally mark HIF-α for VHL-mediated degradation, stabilizing HIF to raise endogenous EPO and improve iron handling (lower hepcidin).

**Myeloid factors.** Filgrastim (short-acting G-CSF), pegfilgrastim (PEGylated, cleared largely by neutrophil-receptor binding, so self-regulating), and sargramostim (GM-CSF). Rare but important: splenic rupture, ARDS, sickle crisis in sickle cell disease.

**Platelet agents.** Romiplostim is a peptibody that binds the TPO receptor's extracellular domain; eltrombopag and avatrombopag are small molecules binding the transmembrane domain. Eltrombopag chelates polyvalent cations (take apart from dairy and antacids) and can cause hepatotoxicity. Plerixafor, a CXCR4 antagonist, augments stem cell mobilization.
levels.phd:
**Oxygen sensing.** The 2019 Nobel Prize recognized the HIF pathway. Under normoxia, PHD2 hydroxylates prolines on HIF-α using O₂, 2-oxoglutarate and Fe²⁺; hydroxylated HIF-α is recognized by the von Hippel–Lindau E3 ligase and degraded. A second hydroxylase, FIH, blocks coactivator binding. In hypoxia, HIF-2α accumulates in renal interstitial fibroblast-like cells (renal EPO-producing cells) and drives EPO transcription. In CKD, these cells transdifferentiate toward myofibroblasts and lose EPO output, the core of renal anemia. HIF-PH inhibitors activate this program pharmacologically and also reduce hepcidin, but HIF targets include VEGF and glycolytic genes, raising theoretical concerns about tumor growth, retinopathy and vascular calcification; cardiovascular safety relative to ESAs has been a central regulatory question, with approvals differing between regions.

**ESA biology versus physiology.** Exogenous ESA dosing produces supraphysiological peaks, and EPO receptors are expressed on endothelium and some tumor cells; whether tumor EPO receptor signaling drives progression has been controversial because of antibody specificity problems in early studies. The thrombotic risk appears related to ESA dose and hemoglobin trajectory, and post-hoc analyses suggest that high ESA doses in hyporesponders may be a marker and a mediator of harm.

**Engineering lessons.** Darbepoetin illustrates glycoengineering: sialic acid content inversely correlates with receptor affinity yet extends half-life, giving greater in vivo potency. Pegfilgrastim illustrates target-mediated drug disposition: clearance via neutrophil G-CSF receptors means drug persists during neutropenic nadir and is cleared during recovery.

**TPO receptor agonists.** Distinct binding sites allow additive use in research and explain species specificity: eltrombopag binds a histidine in the human transmembrane domain, so it is inactive in mice. Beyond ITP, eltrombopag added to immunosuppression improves responses in severe aplastic anemia, suggesting effects on stem cells, possibly including intracellular iron chelation. Long-term concern centers on marrow reticulin fibrosis.
levels.expert:
**ESA practice in CKD.** Before starting, correct iron deficiency (often with IV iron in dialysis patients), exclude B12 or folate deficiency, bleeding, hemolysis and hyperparathyroidism. Aim to reduce transfusion needs and symptoms, not to normalize hemoglobin; guidelines advise against targeting high-normal values because of stroke and cardiovascular events. Control blood pressure, and watch for access thrombosis. If a patient on a stable ESA suddenly develops severe anemia with very low reticulocytes, suspect antibody-mediated pure red cell aplasia: stop the ESA and test for anti-EPO antibodies.

**ESAs in cancer.** Reserve for chemotherapy-induced anemia in non-curative settings after discussing risks; ESAs are generally avoided when cure is the goal because of concerns about tumor progression and survival. Transfusion remains the fastest fix.

**G-CSF practice.** Primary prophylaxis is recommended when the chemotherapy regimen's febrile neutropenia risk is high, or intermediate with patient risk factors such as older age. G-CSF is not a substitute for prompt antibiotics in febrile neutropenia, which remains an emergency. Warn about bone pain (antihistamines are sometimes used), and take left upper quadrant or shoulder-tip pain seriously because of splenic rupture. In sickle cell disease, G-CSF can provoke severe crises; plerixafor-based mobilization is preferred when collecting stem cells for gene therapy.

**ITP and TPO-RAs.** First-line ITP therapy is corticosteroids or IVIG when treatment is needed; TPO-RAs are used for persistent or chronic disease. They don't work immediately, platelets can overshoot, and stopping abruptly causes rebound thrombocytopenia. Monitor liver tests with eltrombopag and separate it from calcium and iron. Avatrombopag and lusutrombopag can raise platelets before procedures in chronic liver disease.

**A safety principle.** All of these agents push a physiological signal harder than the body would. That's why the monitoring plan, the target and the stop rule should be decided before the first dose.

keyPoints: EPO from the kidney drives red cell production via EPO receptor–JAK2–STAT5
ESAs (epoetin, darbepoetin) treat CKD anemia; avoid high targets (stroke, thrombosis)
Check iron first: iron deficiency is the main cause of ESA hyporesponse
G-CSF (filgrastim, pegfilgrastim) prevents febrile neutropenia; causes bone pain
TPO receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) treat chronic ITP
HIF-PH inhibitors stabilize HIF to raise endogenous EPO

lessons.title: Sickle Cell Disease Drugs

levels.kid:
Most red blood cells are round and squishy, like little donuts. They slide easily through tiny tubes in your body.

In **sickle cell disease**, a small change in the instructions for hemoglobin makes the cells turn stiff and curved, like a banana or a farm sickle. These stiff cells get stuck in tiny tubes, and that blocks blood flow. It hurts a lot, and it can hurt organs too.

A medicine called **hydroxyurea** helps the body make a baby kind of hemoglobin that doesn't sickle. Drinking water, staying warm and getting help fast for fever also matter. Some kids can now get a new gene treatment that fixes the problem at the source.
levels.hs:
**Sickle cell disease** is inherited. A single change in the β-globin gene swaps one amino acid (glutamic acid to valine), making **hemoglobin S**. When HbS loses oxygen, it sticks together in long fibers that bend red cells into sickles. Sickled cells are stiff, break apart easily (hemolysis) and block small vessels (**vaso-occlusion**).

Problems include painful crises, acute chest syndrome (a lung emergency), stroke in children, infections (the spleen gets damaged early) and organ damage over time.

Main treatments:
- **Hydroxyurea**: the backbone drug. It increases **fetal hemoglobin (HbF)**, which doesn't join HbS fibers. It reduces pain crises, acute chest syndrome and transfusions, and improves survival. It needs blood count monitoring because it lowers white cells and platelets.
- **L-glutamine**: an amino acid powder that reduces oxidative stress in red cells.
- **Crizanlizumab**: an antibody against P-selectin, a sticky molecule on vessel walls. Its benefit has been questioned by a later trial.
- **Transfusions**: prevent stroke in children with abnormal brain blood flow on ultrasound.
- **Cures**: stem cell transplant from a matched donor, and newer **gene therapies** that either edit cells to make lots of HbF or add a working anti-sickling globin gene.

Supportive care is huge: penicillin and vaccines in young children, folic acid, fluids, fast treatment of fever, and strong pain control during crises.
levels.college:
**Pathophysiology for pharmacology.** Polymerization of deoxy-HbS is extremely concentration-dependent, with a delay time that scales with a very high power of HbS concentration. Small reductions in intracellular HbS concentration, or the presence of non-polymerizing hemoglobin, therefore lengthen the delay enough for cells to escape the microcirculation before sickling. Beyond polymerization, the disease involves hemolysis-driven nitric oxide scavenging by free hemoglobin, endothelial activation, adhesion of red cells, leukocytes and platelets (P-selectin, VCAM-1), and sterile inflammation.

**Hydroxyurea.** An inhibitor of **ribonucleotide reductase**, it causes mild marrow stress that recruits erythroid progenitors with higher γ-globin expression; it also may generate NO and soluble guanylyl cyclase signaling that raises γ-globin. Additional benefits: lower neutrophil counts (less inflammation), larger red cells (lower HbS concentration) and reduced adhesion. Toxicity: myelosuppression (monitored with counts), macrocytosis (expected) and teratogenicity concerns. Trials such as MSH (adults) and BABY HUG (infants) established efficacy; it is now offered from infancy.

**Other agents.**
- **L-glutamine**: raises NAD redox potential in sickle cells to counter oxidative damage.
- **Crizanlizumab**: anti-P-selectin monoclonal antibody that reduced crises in SUSTAIN, but the STAND trial did not confirm superiority over placebo, and European authorization was revoked.
- **Voxelotor**: increased hemoglobin–oxygen affinity to inhibit polymerization; it was withdrawn worldwide in 2024 after data showing excess deaths and crises.

**Transfusion therapy.** Chronic transfusion (simple or exchange) lowers the HbS percentage; the STOP trial showed that transfusion prevents first stroke in children with high transcranial Doppler velocities. Iron overload then requires chelation.

**Curative and gene-based approaches.** Allogeneic stem cell transplantation; **exagamglogene autotemcel** (CRISPR editing of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to derepress γ-globin) and **lovotibeglogene autotemcel** (lentiviral βA-T87Q anti-sickling gene), both requiring myeloablative conditioning with busulfan.
levels.phd:
**Kinetics as a therapeutic lever.** Eaton and Hofrichter showed that HbS gelation follows a double nucleation mechanism with a delay time inversely proportional to roughly the 30th power of supersaturation. This extraordinary dependence means modest therapeutic changes can be clinically decisive: a rise in HbF to around a fifth of total hemoglobin or more, distributed evenly across cells (pancellular rather than heterocellular), substantially protects. It also explains why sickle trait, with lower HbS concentration, rarely causes vaso-occlusion except in extreme conditions, and why coinheritance of α-thalassemia (lower MCHC) modifies the phenotype.

**The γ-globin switch.** After birth, BCL11A and LRF (ZBTB7A) repress γ-globin by binding its promoter; genome-wide association studies of HbF levels led to an erythroid-specific BCL11A enhancer. Editing this enhancer silences BCL11A in red cell precursors only, avoiding its essential roles in lymphocytes and neurons, a celebrated example of translating human genetics into a therapy. Hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin variants map to the same repressor-binding sites, offering natural proof of safety. Pharmacological HbF inducers under study include DNMT1 inhibitors (decitabine with tetrahydrouridine to prevent its deamination), LSD1 inhibitors and HDAC inhibitors.

**Lessons from failure.** Voxelotor raised hemoglobin, a biomarker, yet post-marketing and trial data revealed harm, reinforcing that surrogate endpoints may not capture net benefit, especially when increased oxygen affinity may impair tissue oxygen delivery. Crizanlizumab showed how a positive phase 2 result can fail to replicate. Pyruvate kinase activators (mitapivat, etavopivat) lower 2,3-BPG, increasing oxygen affinity, and raise ATP; they are being tested in sickle cell disease.

**Gene therapy considerations.** Busulfan conditioning carries infertility and malignancy risks; earlier lentiviral programs prompted investigations of myeloid malignancies, attributed largely to conditioning and pre-existing stress hematopoiesis rather than insertional mutagenesis. Access and cost are major ethical questions.
levels.expert:
**Acute pain crisis.** Treat fast: guidelines advise analgesia within an hour of arrival, using individualized pain plans, scheduled opioid analgesia with frequent reassessment, plus non-opioid adjuncts as appropriate. Under-treatment and stigma are documented, serious problems for patients with sickle cell disease. Give fluids judiciously (over-hydration can worsen lung complications), use incentive spirometry to reduce acute chest syndrome, and look for triggers such as infection.

**Red flags.**
- Fever: an emergency because of functional asplenia; draw cultures and give prompt parenteral antibiotics covering encapsulated organisms.
- Acute chest syndrome: new infiltrate with chest pain, fever, hypoxia or respiratory symptoms; treat with antibiotics including atypical cover, oxygen and transfusion (exchange if severe).
- Stroke: sudden weakness, speech change or seizures in a child; urgent imaging and exchange transfusion.
- Splenic sequestration (falling hemoglobin with a large spleen) and aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 (very low reticulocytes).

**Hydroxyurea in practice.** Offer it to all children from about nine months and to adults with frequent crises or acute chest syndrome. Escalate to the maximum tolerated level guided by blood counts, and expect the MCV and HbF to rise as signs of response and adherence. Pregnancy planning is discussed because of teratogenicity concerns.

**Transfusion pearls.** Avoid raising hemoglobin too high, because higher viscosity can trigger vaso-occlusion. Use phenotype-matched units (at least Rh and Kell) to reduce alloimmunization, which is common because donor and recipient populations differ. Watch for delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions, which can mimic a pain crisis and cause hyperhemolysis.

**Prevention for children.** Newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis in early childhood, pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines, and annual transcranial Doppler screening from age two have changed childhood survival dramatically.

keyPoints: HbS (Glu6Val) polymerizes when deoxygenated, causing sickling, hemolysis and vaso-occlusion
Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and raises HbF; monitor counts
L-glutamine reduces oxidative stress; crizanlizumab's benefit is disputed; voxelotor was withdrawn in 2024
Transfusion prevents stroke in children with abnormal transcranial Doppler
Gene therapies: BCL11A enhancer editing and anti-sickling gene addition
Fever is an emergency because of functional asplenia

kidTest.explain: Stuck cells block blood flow, which hurts.

lessons.title: Transfusion-Related Pharmacology

levels.kid:
Sometimes a person loses a lot of blood, or their body can't make enough. Then doctors can give them blood from a kind helper called a **donor**. This is a **transfusion**.

Blood is split into parts, like separating a smoothie. Red cells carry oxygen. Platelets help plug cuts. Plasma is the yellow liquid with clotting helpers.

Doctors check the blood type very carefully, like matching puzzle pieces, so the body doesn't fight the new blood. Some medicines also help blood clot, and some can quickly undo blood thinners in an emergency.
levels.hs:
A **blood transfusion** gives a patient parts of donated blood. Whole blood is separated into **components**, and each one fixes a different problem:
- **Red blood cells**: for severe anemia or major bleeding, to carry oxygen.
- **Platelets**: for very low platelets or bleeding when platelets don't work.
- **Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)**: contains clotting factors.
- **Cryoprecipitate**: rich in fibrinogen.

**Matching** matters. ABO blood groups and the Rh(D) factor are tested, and donor cells are cross-matched with the patient's plasma. Giving the wrong ABO type can cause a deadly reaction where antibodies destroy the donor cells. Group O negative red cells are the emergency choice when there's no time to test.

**Transfusion reactions** include fever, allergic hives, fluid overload (TACO), lung injury (TRALI) and infections (now very rare thanks to screening).

**Pharmacology of bleeding**: Doctors also use drugs instead of, or alongside, blood:
- **Tranexamic acid** blocks clot breakdown and reduces deaths from bleeding in trauma.
- **Vitamin K** and **prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)** reverse warfarin.
- **Idarucizumab** reverses dabigatran; **andexanet alfa** reverses factor Xa inhibitors like apixaban.
- **Protamine** reverses heparin.

Doctors try to give blood only when needed, because it has risks and is a precious donated gift.
levels.college:
**Component therapy.** Red cells are stored refrigerated in an anticoagulant-preservative solution containing **citrate** (which chelates calcium to stop clotting), plus dextrose and adenine. Platelets are stored at room temperature with agitation, which makes bacterial contamination their main infectious risk. FFP contains all coagulation factors; cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII.

**Restrictive thresholds.** Trials (TRICC, FOCUS, TRISS and others) showed that restrictive hemoglobin triggers are as safe as liberal ones for most stable patients; some groups, such as acute coronary syndromes, remain debated.

**Storage lesion and massive transfusion.** Stored red cells leak potassium, lose 2,3-BPG (raising oxygen affinity) and accumulate microparticles. Massive transfusion causes:
- Hypocalcemia from citrate load (the liver normally clears citrate; shock impairs this).
- Hyperkalemia, especially with rapid infusion of older units.
- Hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy and acidosis (the "lethal triad" with hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy).
Balanced ratios of plasma, platelets and red cells (PROPPR) and early tranexamic acid (CRASH-2) are standard in trauma.

**Reactions by mechanism.**
- Acute hemolytic: preformed anti-A/B IgM, complement activation, intravascular hemolysis, often from clerical error.
- Febrile non-hemolytic: cytokines from donor leukocytes; reduced by leukoreduction.
- Anaphylaxis: e.g. IgA-deficient recipients with anti-IgA.
- TRALI: donor anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies activate recipient neutrophils in the lung; reduced by using male-donor plasma.
- TACO: hydrostatic pulmonary edema from volume.
- Transfusion-associated GVHD: viable donor T cells engraft; prevented by irradiation for at-risk recipients.

**Reversal agents.** Vitamin K (slow, restores synthesis), 4-factor PCC (II, VII, IX, X plus proteins C and S; rapid), idarucizumab (humanized Fab binding dabigatran), andexanet alfa (decoy factor Xa) and protamine (polycation neutralizing heparin; partial against LMWH).
levels.phd:
**Antifibrinolytics.** Tranexamic acid is a lysine analogue that occupies lysine-binding sites on plasminogen kringle domains, preventing its binding to fibrin and so inhibiting fibrinolysis. CRASH-2 found mortality benefit in trauma only when given early; late administration was associated with harm, possibly reflecting a shift from hyperfibrinolysis to fibrinolysis shutdown after injury. WOMAN showed reduced bleeding deaths in postpartum hemorrhage; HALT-IT found no benefit in GI bleeding and more venous thrombosis, a reminder that mechanism does not guarantee benefit in every context.

**Hemostatic resuscitation science.** Trauma-induced coagulopathy is not just dilution: tissue hypoperfusion activates protein C and degrades the endothelial glycocalyx, causing anticoagulation and fibrinolysis. Viscoelastic tests (thromboelastography, rotational thromboelastometry) allow goal-directed replacement with fibrinogen concentrate, PCC or platelets.

**Molecular design of reversal agents.**
- Idarucizumab binds dabigatran with an affinity far higher than dabigatran's affinity for thrombin; it is renally cleared.
- Andexanet is a recombinant, catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy lacking the membrane-binding Gla domain; it sequesters Xa inhibitors but can also bind tissue factor pathway inhibitor, which may contribute to thrombotic events. ANNEXA-I in intracerebral hemorrhage improved hemostatic efficacy but increased thrombotic events, and debate continues over whether it beats PCC.
- Ciraparantag, a small synthetic cation, is in development as a broad reversal agent.

**Immunology of compatibility.** Naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B are IgM that fix complement, explaining the violence of ABO-incompatible reactions, whereas Rh and Kell alloantibodies are usually IgG from prior exposure, causing extravascular hemolysis and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitization of RhD-negative mothers, a triumph of preventive immunopharmacology. Pathogen-reduction technologies (amotosalen with UVA, riboflavin with UV) crosslink nucleic acids to inactivate pathogens and leukocytes in platelets and plasma.
levels.expert:
**Before you transfuse.** Ask what the problem is: oxygen delivery, active bleeding, or a lab number. Most stable inpatients do well with a restrictive threshold, and one red cell unit at a time with reassessment is common practice. Iron-deficient but stable patients often need iron, not blood. Patient blood management (treating anemia before surgery, cell salvage, tranexamic acid, minimizing blood draws) reduces exposure.

**Bedside safety.** Most fatal hemolytic reactions come from identification errors: the wrong sample in the tube or the wrong bag at the bedside. Two-person or electronic verification is the safeguard. If a patient develops fever, pain at the infusion site, back pain, hypotension or dark urine, stop the transfusion immediately, keep the line open with saline, recheck identity, and send the bag and samples to the blood bank.

**Distinguishing TRALI and TACO.** Both cause breathlessness within hours. TACO points to volume: hypertension, raised jugular pressure, positive fluid balance, raised natriuretic peptide and response to diuretics. TRALI tends toward fever and hypotension with normal filling pressures; treatment is supportive, and diuretics may harm. Report both so donors can be investigated.

**Massive bleeding.** Activate the massive transfusion protocol early, give tranexamic acid early in trauma, use balanced ratios, then switch to lab-guided therapy. Check ionized calcium and potassium repeatedly, warm all fluids, and treat acidosis by restoring perfusion.

**Anticoagulant emergencies.**
- Warfarin with major bleeding: 4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K (PCC is fast but short-lived; vitamin K sustains the effect).
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab.
- Apixaban or rivaroxaban: andexanet or PCC, depending on local protocols.
- Heparin: protamine, given slowly to avoid hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions.

**Special products.** Irradiated components for stem cell transplant recipients, some patients on purine analogues, and intrauterine or neonatal exchange transfusions; CMV-safe products for vulnerable groups; washed products for recurrent severe allergic reactions.

keyPoints: Components: red cells, platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen)
Restrictive transfusion thresholds are safe for most stable patients
Citrate causes hypocalcemia in massive transfusion; stored cells add potassium
TRALI is antibody-mediated; TACO is volume overload
Reversal: vitamin K + PCC (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet (Xa), protamine (heparin)
Tranexamic acid inhibits fibrinolysis; give early in trauma
